name: Polyethylene
description: A polyolefin thermoplastic widely used in medical tubing and device components, valued for chemical inertness, flexibility across grades, and consistent performance in RF-based thermal forming.
long_description: Polyethylene (PE) is a thermoplastic polymer made by polymerizing ethylene monomer, available in various density grades (e.g., LDPE, HDPE) with corresponding differences in stiffness. In catheter manufacturing, it’s used especially in cost-sensitive or single-use devices requiring flexible tubing or low-friction surfaces. Different grades range from fairly soft (low-density PE) to relatively rigid (high-density PE), allowing designers to tailor catheter sections or components for flexibility or support as needed. In RF-driven processes—such as catheter tip forming, flaring, and thermal bonding—polyethylene’s relatively low melting range and predictable thermal behavior enable it to soften and re-solidify under controlled conditions, yielding consistent tip geometries and welds when heat and cooling are properly managed. Its low surface energy means PE bonds best to itself, often necessitating surface treatment or tie-layers to join with other polymers. Sterilization compatibility (e.g., EtO, limited gamma) and biocompatibility depend on the specific grade and any additives; medical-grade PE resins are widely available, and their suitability should be confirmed via supplier documentation and device-level validation.

properties.radiopacity: Not inherently radiopaque; often compounded with radiopaque fillers such as barium sulfate or tungsten if needed

applications: Catheter tipping (forming soft distal tips on polyethylene-based catheters or tubing)
Catheter flaring (expanding PE tubing ends for connectors or assembly interfaces)
Joining tubing segments (thermal welding of PE-to-PE catheter segments)
Forming smooth transitions or neckdowns in polyethylene catheter shafts

process_notes.thermal_processability: Melts at relatively low temperatures and responds well to RF heating, allowing easy forming of tips and flares when process parameters are dialed in.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Polyethylene welds readily to itself under heat; however, its low surface energy makes bonding to dissimilar polymers challenging without surface treatments or adhesive tie-layers.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Softer grades can become quite pliable when molten and may stick to tooling; careful control of heat, use of release coatings, and adequate cooling/holding fixtures help maintain shape and dimensional accuracy as the PE solidifies (especially accounting for shrinkage in higher-density grades).

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Polyethylene (including LDPE and HDPE) is widely used in medical devices and packaging. Medical-grade formulations with minimal additives are generally considered biocompatible for short-term contact, but specific grade certification (e.g., USP Class VI or ISO 10993 compliance) and device-level biocompatibility testing are recommended to ensure regulatory suitability.

name: Polyvinyl chloride
description: PVC is a versatile, low-cost catheter material known for flexibility, clarity, and ease of processing. Medical PVC can be soft or semi-rigid depending on additives, and is used in tubing and fluid bags. Newer formulations often use DEHP-free plasticizers due to health concerns.
long_description: Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is an amorphous vinyl polymer widely used for medical tubing and components due to its versatility and ease of processing. Flexible PVC formulations (with plasticizers) yield high elongation (often >300%) and clarity, making them suitable for endotracheal tubes, IV catheters, and bag materials. PVC’s polar molecular structure allows it to couple well with RF induction heating for forming and welding. In catheter tip forming, PVC can be heated and shaped (typically ~150°C) into smooth inner/outer radii with short cycle times. Similarly, RF bonding or heat sealing can join PVC layers or seal bags due to dielectric heating. Without stabilizers, PVC can decompose before fully melting, so medical grades use additive packages to reduce charring and discoloration. PVC’s continuous service temperature is limited (often cited around 50–60°C depending on formulation). Medical-grade PVC is available in DEHP-free grades to address toxicity and leachables concerns; sterilization is typically by EtO or gamma (steam is generally only suitable for rigid grades). Biocompatibility and regulatory compliance should be confirmed for each formulation.

properties.durometer_range: Shore A ~60 (soft plasticized) up to Shore D ~70–80 (rigid)
properties.elongation: 60–450% (up to ~450% for highly plasticized grades; ~60% for unplasticized PVC)
properties.radiopacity: Typically clear; radiopaque fillers (barium sulfate, tungsten) added if needed

applications: Catheter tipping (soft or atraumatic distal tips)
Catheter flaring (expanding tube ends for connectors)
RF heat sealing of medical bags (IV/blood bags)

process_notes.thermal_processability: PVC heats and softens at relatively low temperatures (~150°C). Plasticized grades flow predictably under RF heating, enabling rapid forming and sealing. Care is needed to prevent overheating, as PVC can decompose and char at elevated temperatures. Its polar nature supports efficient coupling with RF energy, making RF-induced forming and welding fast and controllable.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: RF welding bonds PVC well to itself and can work well with other polar plastics; joining to nonpolar polymers (e.g., PE, PP) usually requires adhesives, tie layers, or surface treatment. Chemical resistance is generally good for many aqueous fluids, but compatibility and extractables/leachables depend strongly on the additive package.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: PVC can become tacky when heated; polished stainless-steel dies and controlled cooling help prevent sticking. Short RF cycle times and controlled insertion depth help reduce lumen collapse. Tooling should account for shrinkage and maintain alignment during forming and sealing.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade PVC is widely used in catheters, IV/blood bags, and tubing. Biocompatibility depends on the plasticizer and additive package; DEHP-free PVC is commonly used to reduce leachables concerns. Suppliers typically provide regulatory and biocompatibility support documentation; device manufacturers should verify the specific grade and perform testing appropriate to the intended use.

name: Polyether Block Amide
description: A thermoplastic elastomer family widely used in catheter shafts and distal features, valued for tunable stiffness and consistent performance in RF-based forming and joining.
long_description: PEBAX (also referred to as PEBA) is a block-copolymer thermoplastic elastomer made from polyether and polyamide segments. In catheter development, it’s frequently selected because grades span from very flexible to relatively stiff, enabling soft distal features, supportive proximal sections, and controlled transitions along the device. In RF-driven processes—such as catheter tipping, flaring, and segment-to-segment joining—PEBAX offers predictable softening and re-solidification behavior that supports repeatable geometry and smooth surface finish when heat input, alignment, and cooling are well controlled. Sterilization suitability and biocompatibility are grade- and supplier-dependent, so medical-device programs typically confirm these through supplier documentation and device-level validation.

properties.radiopacity: Often compounded with radiopaque fillers such as barium sulfate or tungsten (formulation-dependent)

applications: Catheter tipping (soft or atraumatic distal features)
Catheter flaring (expanded ends for interfaces and assemblies)
Joining catheter segments (PEBAX-to-PEBAX transitions and assemblies)
Forming smooth transitions between catheter sections

process_notes.thermal_processability: Responds well to controlled RF heating for forming and joining, supporting consistent geometry across production when the process window is dialed in.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Typically joins well to itself; joining to dissimilar polymers is application-dependent and may require a compatible intermediate layer or surface preparation.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Some grades can become tacky during forming; development often focuses on heat input, dwell, release strategy, and cooling to prevent sticking and maintain concentricity.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: PEBAX is offered in medical-grade formulations by major suppliers. Biocompatibility and regulatory suitability depend on the specific grade, additives, and supplier documentation, and should be confirmed as part of the device’s validation plan.

name: Thermoplastic Polyurethane
description: Medical-grade thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) combines biocompatibility, flexibility, and durability, making it suitable for complex catheter designs and distal tip features.
long_description: Polyurethane (PU) used in catheters is typically a thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) elastomer. Grades range from very soft (for atraumatic tips) to relatively firm (for catheter shafts), achieved by tuning soft and hard segments in the polymer. TPU offers high tensile strength and elasticity, helping maintain lumen integrity under bending or stress. Its polar structure makes TPU compatible with RF heating, so processes like RF tipping, flaring, and welding can produce repeatable shapes with smooth finishes when process parameters are well controlled. Medical TPUs are formulated to meet biocompatibility and sterilization standards (typically ISO 10993 and USP Class VI), though exact certification depends on the grade and supplier; device programs usually verify this via documentation and testing.

properties.durometer_range: Shore A ~60–95 for softer grades up to Shore D ~50–70 for stiffer catheter sections (grade-dependent).
properties.water_absorption_24h: ≈1.1–1.5% (24-hour water soak, typical for polyether TPU).
properties.radiopacity: Often compounded (~10–20% loading) with radiopaque fillers (e.g. barium sulfate, tungsten) to make catheters visible under X-ray.

applications: Catheter flaring (expanded proximal ends for fittings)
Segment bonding (RF or thermal welding of catheter sections)
Medical package sealing (RF welding of TPU films for IV/blood bags)

process_notes.thermal_processability: TPU can be extruded or molded; tip/flaring uses heat (~160–200°C) to soften the polymer. In RF tip-forming, only the mold is heated (fast cycle ~2–5s), which localizes heat and helps preserve TPU properties.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: TPU bonds well to itself via RF welding or adhesives due to its polar chemistry. Bonding to dissimilar polymers may require primers or specialized adhesives.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: As with other RF-formed polymers, uniform mold alignment and controlled cooling are critical for consistent geometry and surface quality. TPU can become tacky if overheated, so tooling often uses release coatings or cooling to prevent sticking and maintain concentricity.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade TPU is available from major suppliers with formulations to meet ISO 10993-1 and USP Class VI requirements. Regulatory and biocompatibility testing is grade-specific; programs should confirm suitability (e.g. long-term implant vs. short-term use) per device requirements.

name: Thermoplastic Elastomer
description: TPE blends the elastic flexibility of rubber with the processing ease of thermoplastics.
long_description: Thermoplastic elastomers cover a wide range of polymers (polyurethane, olefinic, styrenic, etc.) that provide rubber-like compliance with thermoplastic processability. In catheter development, medical-grade TPEs (such as TPU and polyether block amide) are selected for their adjustable flexibility, strength, and kink resistance. Under RF or induction heating, TPE tubing will soften and re-solidify predictably, enabling smooth tip forming and flaring. For example, application reports describe shaping certain TPE catheter tips by heating an induction die to roughly 210°C for a few seconds. TPE-based adhesives and overmolding resins are used to bond catheter segments and add soft distal features. TPE films are also weldable for packaging; they can be RF-sealed into sterile pouches and bag ports.

properties.durometer_range: Shore hardness from ~5A (very soft) up to ~80A or D70 (stiffer grades, type-dependent)
properties.radiopacity: Normally transparent; often compounded with radiopaque fillers (e.g., barium sulfate or tungsten) if needed

applications: Catheter tipping (soft or atraumatic distal tips)
Catheter flaring (proximal end expansion for connectors or hubs)
Joining catheter segments (TPE welding and adhesive bonding)
Soft overmolding (adding flexible grips or coatings on catheter shafts)
Sterile bag/pouch sealing (RF welding of TPE films for medical packaging)

process_notes.thermal_processability: Softens under RF or induction heating like other thermoplastics. Certain TPE formulations can be tip-formed using an induction-heated die around ~210°C for a few seconds, depending on geometry and grade.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Bonds readily to itself via heat welding and can also be joined by ultrasonic welding for some grades. Specialized medical-grade adhesives are commonly used for catheter tubing and tips. Bonding to dissimilar materials often requires primers, tie-layers, surface treatment, or adhesives.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Some TPE formulations can become tacky if overheated; polished dies, appropriate venting, controlled heat input, and managed cooling help maintain geometry and support clean release.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade TPE compounds are available that can be supplied to meet ISO 10993 and/or USP Class VI expectations. Final device-level biocompatibility and sterilization suitability should be confirmed for the selected grade, process, and finished device.

name: Polytetrafluoroethylene
description: PTFE is a lubricious, chemically inert fluoropolymer often used as a catheter inner lining to create a smooth, low-friction lumen for guidewires and devices.
long_description:
Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE, often known by the brand name Teflon) is a fully fluorinated polymer prized for its exceptional chemical inertness and extremely low coefficient of friction. It can remain stable at high temperatures (theoretically melting at ~327°C) but is not melt-processable, so catheter-grade PTFE liners are made by powder sintering or advanced extrusion. The base material is relatively soft and low-strength, so manufacturers produce ultra-thin-walled PTFE tubes that give good tensile strength while preserving flexibility.

In catheter design, PTFE's lubricity provides a near-frictionless inner lumen, aiding guidewire passage and minimizing vessel trauma. However, PTFE resists bonding to other polymers without surface treatment. Many liners are manufactured with etched surfaces or tie-layers to allow adhesives or overmolding. When forming catheter tips or flares with RF induction, PTFE-lined sections do not soften or melt (dielectric loss is negligible), so the PTFE liner is typically retracted or removed at the distal end to allow the outer polymer to be shaped without interference.

Likewise, PTFE cannot be directly welded by RF energy (it neither heats nor fuses under RF). Instead, PTFE films or fabrics serve as high-temperature, non-stick covers on RF or impulse heat-sealing electrodes, preventing polymer melt from adhering. Medical-grade PTFE is available from major suppliers and is chemically inert, but its susceptibility to ionizing radiation means gamma or e-beam sterilization is generally avoided.

process_notes.thermal_processability: PTFE does not heat or melt under typical RF induction (negligible dielectric loss). It requires temperatures near 327°C to soften, so RF tip-forming does not affect PTFE liners.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: PTFE’s inert surface resists adhesion. It must be surface-treated (e.g. etching, plasma) or paired with tie-layers to allow adhesives or over-molding. Even treated PTFE often requires specialized adhesives or mechanical interlocks for secure bonding.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: PTFE’s low friction and thermal stability make it ideal as a non-stick tool covering. PTFE sheets or coated fabrics are commonly applied to RF/heat-sealer electrodes to prevent sticking. During catheter forming, PTFE liners are usually retracted from heated zones to avoid distortion.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade PTFE formulations (often USP Class VI) are widely available and biocompatible. PTFE is inert and well-tolerated in catheters and implants. Note: PTFE can degrade under gamma or e-beam sterilization, so EtO or steam sterilization is preferred.

name: Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene
description: FEP is a melt-processable fluoropolymer used in medical devices, notably catheters. It is softer and more flexible than PTFE, with high optical clarity and low friction. Its lower melting point allows it to be extruded into thin-walled tubing and heat-shrink sleeves for catheter layers.
long_description: FEP (Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene) is a melt-processable copolymer of tetrafluoroethylene and hexafluoropropylene introduced as a thermoplastic alternative to PTFE. Unlike PTFE, FEP can be extruded into continuous tubing and heat-formed into complex shapes. It exhibits very low chemical reactivity, excellent UV resistance, and naturally low surface friction. Because of its lower melting point (~260°C) and transparency, FEP is often used in catheters as a lubricious liner or heat-shrinkable outer sheath. In catheter construction, FEP heat-shrink tubing can be used to reflow (bond) softer materials (like PEBAX or nylon) in a catheter shaft, for example to create atraumatic tip sleeves. As a thermoplastic, FEP also supports RF-driven forming: segments of FEP tubing can be tipped, tapered, flared or flanged by heating a metal die or mandrel (typically via induction) to melt the FEP. However, FEP’s chemical inertness means it does not readily weld to itself or other polymers without surface treatment; processes like plasma etching or specialized adhesives are often needed for bonding. FEP can withstand common sterilization methods (EtO, gamma, steam, E-beam) without degradation.

properties.radiopacity: Requires addition of radiopaque fillers (e.g. BaSO4, Bi2O3, W) for visibility

applications: Catheter and introducer liners/sheaths (e.g. vascular, urologic, epidural)
Atraumatic tip coverings (heat-shrink sleeves for soft-tipped catheter ends)
Flared or flanged tube ends for catheter hubs/connectors (via thermal forming)
Joining/bonding of catheter segments (FEP-to-FEP or FEP-to-other materials, typically with primers or adhesives)
Medical tubing for chemical/fluid transfer (inert, high-purity liners)
RF heat sealing and film welding (limited use; FEP’s low dielectric loss means it's not easily RF-weldable)

process_notes.thermal_processability: As a thermoplastic, FEP softens at ~260°C and flows under heat. In RF induction processes, energy is absorbed by the metal tooling rather than the polymer, so FEP often requires higher temperature and longer dwell to form. If controlled, it yields consistent, smooth geometry.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: FEP is highly inert; it resists welding to itself or other polymers without special treatment. Bonding typically requires surface preparation (etching, plasma) and specialized adhesives or primers to achieve adhesion.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Tooling must withstand high temperatures (~300°C) and should have polished, low-friction surfaces to aid release. Rapid cooling (air or water) is applied after forming to set shape; uncontrolled shrinkage or sticking can distort features.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: FEP has a proven history of use in medical devices. Medical-grade FEP (often USP Class VI/ISO 10993-certified) is available from major suppliers. Its chemical inertness and thermal stability generally provide good biocompatibility, and FEP tolerates EtO, gamma, e-beam and steam sterilization. Material-specific biocompatibility (cytotoxicity, leachables, etc.) should be verified per device requirements.

name: Polyamide (Nylon)
description: A strong, semi-rigid polymer family used in catheter shafts and distal tips. Nylons (polyamides) provide high tensile strength, excellent abrasion resistance, and kink resistance, with predictable thermal-forming behavior suited to RF-based tip forming, flaring, and bonding operations.
long_description:
Polyamide (commonly called Nylon) is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic used in many catheter components. Medical-grade nylons (e.g. PA 11, PA 12) offer a balance of stiffness and flexibility: they form strong proximal shafts yet can be heat-formed into soft distal tips. Nylon tubing is valued for its high tensile strength, abrasion resistance, and reliable melting/re-solidification behavior. Typical catheter nylons can be thermo-fused to compatible materials; for example, Nylon 12 is often thermally bonded to adjacent segments in catheter assemblies.

Under RF or induction heating, nylon softens uniformly and re-solidifies to retain precise molded shapes. Processing typically occurs around 190–230°C. Because nylon is hygroscopic, thorough drying (e.g. 80–100°C for several hours) is required to remove moisture and avoid defects like splay or brittle parts. Mold tooling is often pre-heated (e.g. ~35–40°C) to ensure controlled crystallization and surface finish. When melted, nylon bonds strongly to itself; joining to dissimilar polymers usually requires adhesives or transition layers.

Beyond catheter components, nylon films (often in polyamide laminates) are used in medical packaging. In RF welding, nylon is commonly used in multilayer pouch and bag structures where strong, consistent seals are required for sterilization packaging or fluid containment. Medical-grade nylons are available (e.g., ISO 10993/USP Class VI grades), but biocompatibility and sterilization compatibility depend on the specific grade and additives. Common sterilization methods include EtO and gamma radiation; some nylon formulations can also tolerate steam, but this varies by formulation and must be verified for each device.

properties.elongation: 25–200% (unfilled grades; depends on type and condition)
properties.water_absorption_24h: 0.5–3.0% (varies by polyamide type; e.g. PA11 <1%, PA12 <2%)
properties.radiopacity: Typically radiolucent; often compounded with barium sulfate or tungsten for imaging visibility if needed

applications: Catheter flaring (flared proximal ends for connectors)
Stiff proximal catheter shafts or support sections
RF sealing of medical packaging films/pouches

process_notes.thermal_processability: Nylon heats and forms reliably under RF induction when properly controlled. Standard forming temperatures are ~200°C. Moisture must be removed beforehand (drying at ~80–100°C) to prevent defects. Cooling and mold temperature control (e.g. ~35–40°C) are critical to lock in geometry.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Nylon fuses well to itself, creating strong welds under heat. Some nylon grades can thermally bond to compatible polymers, but bonds to dissimilar materials (e.g. TPU, PTFE) typically require adhesives or intermediate layers.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Polished metal molds or dies and proper cooling are needed to prevent sticking and ensure smooth surfaces. The tooling is often temperature-controlled to maintain part quality. Overheating or excessive dwell may cause nylon to degrade or crystallize unevenly.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade nylon (e.g. PA11, PA12, PA6/6) is offered by major suppliers. Biocompatibility and regulatory compliance (ISO 10993, USP Class VI, etc.) depend on the specific grade, fillers, and processing aids. Device makers should verify material certifications and include nylon in their biocompatibility validation.

name: Polyimide
description: A high-performance, rigid polymer used for thin-wall catheter tubing and reinforcement. Polyimide provides exceptional tensile strength and high heat and chemical resistance, enabling ultra-thin, high-pressure lumens and support shafts.
long_description: Polyimides (PI) are high-performance polymers known for their thermal, chemical, and mechanical stability. Medical-grade PI tubing or liners can be produced in extremely thin walls (down to ~0.0005") with high tensile strength and burst pressure, enabling use in micro- and balloon catheter designs where small diameter and high pressure tolerance are critical. Since PI does not melt like thermoplastics, tip forming relies on heating near or above PI’s glass transition temperature (~360–400°C) with tight process control. PI is often combined with softer materials: for example, thin PI liners can be laminated inside polyurethane or Pebax shafts to improve column strength and reduce lumen friction. Multi-layer constructions may also pair a lubricious inner layer with a bondable outer PI layer to balance low-friction performance and assembly needs. Reinforced PI tubing (braid or coil) is also used when additional torque transmission and kink performance are required. Overall, PI’s stable profile (high heat tolerance, low creep, chemical resistance) makes it well-suited for demanding catheter components, though its rigidity and high processing temperature require careful control in forming and bonding.

properties.radiopacity: Low (amber polymer); radiopaque fillers added as needed

applications: Catheter distal tip forming (rigid high-temperature tips)
Liners in composite catheter shafts (for low friction and strength)

process_notes.thermal_processability: Thermoset nature means no true melt; forming requires heating around PI’s Tg (~360–400°C) with precise control. RF induction can achieve rapid heating and cooling for localized forming when tooling and feedback are designed for these temperatures.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Polyimide does not readily fuse to itself or to many other polymers by simple heat. Joining typically relies on adhesives, surface preparation, or mechanical interlocks, and multi-layer designs often incorporate a thermoplastic tie layer or bondable outer layer to support assembly.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Molds/dies must withstand very high temperatures. Precise temperature feedback is critical to avoid scorching. Very thin-walled PI tubes need controlled insertion, dwell, and cooling to prevent distortion.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade polyimide is available and is commonly used in catheter components. Many commercially available PI tubing products are offered in grades intended to support USP Class VI and/or ISO 10993 testing, but biocompatibility depends on the specific grade, additives, and processing history. Final device validation should confirm material compliance for the intended use.

name: Polypropylene
description: A lightweight, rigid polyolefin with excellent chemical resistance and dimensional stability. Common in catheter components like introducer dilators and connector hubs (luer fittings) where stiffness and low cost are needed.
long_description: Polypropylene (PP) is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic formed from propylene monomers, resulting in a mostly non-polar polymer with a methyl group on every other carbon. Typical medical-grade homopolymers melt around 160–165 °C and exhibit moderate hardness (Shore D ≈55–65). Mechanically, PP is reasonably strong (yield ~4,500 psi) with good ductility (elongation often >100%). Its high crystallinity gives good heat resistance (service up to ~100 °C) and extremely low moisture uptake (<0.01%), but also means parts can shrink on cooling and require careful mold release. In RF-based processes, PP’s lack of polar groups makes it a poor dielectric heater: it couples weakly to RF energy and typically needs specialized setups or additives for effective welding or tip forming. Standard medical-grade PP is available (e.g., USP Class VI / ISO 10993 compliant) and is considered biocompatible and inert, but final device suitability must be validated by material and regulatory data.

properties.radiopacity: Not intrinsically radiopaque; typically compounded with barium sulfate or tungsten fillers for X-ray visibility

applications: Luer connectors and hub fittings (connector assemblies)
Proximal catheter shaft segments requiring stiffness
General tubing for non-critical fluid paths

process_notes.thermal_processability: PP softens at a well-defined melting point (~160 °C) and can be formed by heating, but its non-polar structure makes direct RF heating inefficient. In practice, an RF-heated die or hot-plate is used to melt PP for flaring or forming, with careful control of heat input and cooling to avoid uneven crystallization.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: PP can be thermally welded to itself (e.g., by hot-plate or extrusion welding) with good strength, but its low surface energy resists bonding to dissimilar materials. RF welding of PP is possible only with special formulations or high energy (often requiring surface treatments or additives). Adhesives or mechanical interlocks are often used when joining PP to other polymers.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: PP shrinks on cooling (often ~1–2%) and does not absorb moisture (stability <0.01% water uptake), but its high crystallinity can cause warpage if cooled too quickly. Molds and dies should allow release (e.g., polished surfaces or release agents) and be heated or cooled uniformly. Precise cooling control helps maintain concentricity and prevent cracking.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: Medical-grade polypropylene is offered by major suppliers and used in many device components. It is generally biologically inert (chemically resistant and non-toxic). Specific biocompatibility claims depend on the grade and additives, so final device validation (per ISO 10993) is required.

name: High-Density Polyethylene
description: A linear, high-crystallinity polyethylene known for its higher stiffness and strength, used in more rigid catheter sections or flares, valued for its durability and stable performance in RF thermal forming and welding.
long_description: HDPE (High-Density Polyethylene) is a polyethylene grade with minimal branching in its polymer chains, resulting in higher crystallinity, density (~0.94–0.96 g/cc), and a melting point around 130–137°C, all higher than those of LDPE. This structure gives HDPE significantly greater rigidity, tensile strength, and chemical resistance. In catheter manufacturing, HDPE is utilized for components that need more support or pushability – for example, stiffer proximal shaft sections, flared tube ends that must hold their shape for connections, or other parts where a harder polymer is beneficial. While not as flexible as LDPE or elastomers, HDPE provides structural integrity and is often used in combination with softer segments in multi-layer or multi-durometer catheter designs. In RF-based thermal forming and bonding, HDPE requires more energy (higher temperature) to soften due to its higher melting point, but once heated it can be molded into precise shapes (such as robust flares or tip forms) and welded to itself reliably. It cools into a firm shape; because of its crystallinity, some shrinkage can occur upon cooling, so process parameters and tool design account for this to maintain final dimensions. HDPE’s inertness gives it excellent chemical compatibility and it withstands EtO sterilization easily. It can also be gamma sterilized, though high radiation doses may induce slight embrittlement over time (a common trait of polyolefins). HDPE is not suitable for high-temperature steam sterilization, as it will soften or deform near autoclave temperatures. Medical-grade HDPE resins (including certain FDA/USP Class VI compliant grades) are widely used in healthcare products; nevertheless, each specific formulation’s biocompatibility and regulatory compliance should be confirmed through supplier documentation and device-level testing, especially if any fillers or additives are present.

sterilization_methods: Steam (not suitable at standard autoclave temps)
properties.radiopacity: Not intrinsically radiopaque; often requires blending with radiopaque fillers (e.g., barium sulfate or tungsten) if fluoroscopic visibility is needed

applications: Catheter proximal sections (using HDPE tubing for stiff, supportive shaft sections to improve pushability)
Catheter flaring (forming rigid, durable flares on HDPE tubing ends for connector interfaces or strain reliefs)
Joining HDPE segments (thermal welding of HDPE-to-HDPE tubing in catheter assembly)
Forming tapered or stepped transitions in catheter shafts where a more rigid segment is required

process_notes.thermal_processability: Needs higher heat input than LDPE to reach melt, but responds predictably to RF heating; once softened, HDPE can be formed and welded with good repeatability, then solidifies into a rigid shape upon cooling.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Thermal welding of HDPE to itself produces strong bonds. Like other polyethylenes, its low surface energy and crystallinity make adhesive bonding or bonding to different polymers difficult without special surface treatments or adhesive intermediates.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: HDPE’s higher stiffness means less risk of sticking than very soft plastics, but its tendency to shrink upon cooling (due to crystallization) means molds should be designed for proper shrink allowance and even cooling. Securing the part in the tool until it sufficiently cools helps ensure the formed geometry (e.g., flare or tip) retains its intended dimensions and shape without warping or stress cracks.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: HDPE is widely used for medical device components and packaging, and many grades are available in medical/food-safe formulations. The polymer’s inherent inertness and history of use (including in implants like UHMWPE) suggest good biocompatibility for appropriately chosen grades. Still, any specific HDPE grade used in a device should have supporting biocompatibility documentation (such as ISO 10993 or USP Class VI test results) from the supplier, and final device testing should confirm that it meets all required biocompatibility and regulatory standards for its intended use.

name: Ethylene Tetrafluoroethylene
description: ETFE combines high mechanical strength, abrasion resistance, and chemical stability, often used as a liner or jacket for catheters requiring durability and biocompatibility.

name: Low-Density Polyethylene
description: A branched, low-density form of polyethylene known for its softness and flexibility, often used in pliable catheter tips and sections, valued for its low melting point and ease of RF tip forming.
long_description: LDPE (Low-Density Polyethylene) is a polyethylene variant characterized by a high degree of long-chain branching, which yields a lower density, lower crystallinity, and a melting point around 105–115°C. This structure makes LDPE a very soft and flexible polymer. In catheter manufacturing, LDPE is selected for applications that require a very pliable material, such as atraumatic distal tips, soft sleeves, or flexible tubing sections. Its low durometer and melting temperature allow it to form smooth, atraumatic tips or flares at relatively low RF energy, though its lower strength means it’s generally used in less mechanically demanding portions of a device. During RF-based tipping or flaring, LDPE softens quickly and flows easily into molds, and with proper cooling it re-solidifies to a smooth finish. Because it is so soft when molten, process control (minimal heat input, short dwell time, and supportive mandrels or molds) is important to maintain concentricity and prevent over-melting or sticking. LDPE is chemically inert and compatible with common gas sterilization (EtO) and usually tolerant of gamma sterilization for single-use products (though radiation may cause some embrittlement). It cannot withstand standard steam autoclaving due to its low melting point. Medical-grade LDPE resins are available for use in healthcare products, but the specific grade’s biocompatibility and any additives should be verified via supplier documentation and device-level testing.

sterilization_methods: Steam (not recommended due to low melt point)
properties.radiopacity: Not inherently radiopaque; can be compounded with radiopaque fillers (e.g., barium sulfate or tungsten) if X-ray visibility is required

applications: Catheter tipping (atraumatic soft tips formed from LDPE for gentle distal ends)
Catheter flaring (creating flared ends on LDPE tubing for connector interfaces or soft transitions)
Joining LDPE segments (thermal welding of LDPE tube sections in catheter assemblies)
Forming flexible transitions or tapers in multi-durometer catheter shafts using LDPE

process_notes.thermal_processability: Very low melting point and softening temperature, which means LDPE responds quickly to RF heating and is easily formed; precise low heat input and short dwell ensure controlled molding without overheating.
process_notes.bonding_behavior: Fuses readily to itself under heat (LDPE-to-LDPE bonds), but like all polyethylene it has a non-polar, low-energy surface, making adhesive or thermal bonding to other plastics difficult without primers or surface activation.
process_notes.tooling_considerations: Because LDPE becomes extremely soft and pliable when molten, it can stick to tooling or deform under its own weight. Molds/dies often use polished surfaces or release coatings, and the process may include immediate cooling or supportive mandrels to preserve shape and concentricity as the part solidifies.

biocompatibility.usage_scope: LDPE is commonly used in medical tubing, bags, and disposable device components. Medical-grade LDPE (with FDA or ISO 10993 compliance) should be used for body-contact applications. The base polymer is chemically inert and generally biocompatible for temporary contact, but any additives (antioxidants, colorants) and the specific grade’s certifications must be verified to ensure it meets the necessary biocompatibility and regulatory standards for the intended use.

name: Polyether Ether Ketone
description: PEEK is a high-performance polymer offering exceptional strength, stiffness, and temperature resistance. It is used in demanding catheter components where precision and durability are critical.
